title: Zašto je teško?
theme: A map of four systems. English keeps the word still. Bosnian dresses it again.
reviewerNotes: Orientation plus a fat map of piles, jobs, matching, and doing-words. No full charts.

whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: This chapter is the map of the notebook, not a full Bosnian grammar lesson. You may already know Ana’s Book 1 line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. That line is the same drink as kahva, with a different ending because the job in the sentence changed. When you close the laptop you should know what this book will teach, and what it will wait on. English hides the work in little words like the and to. Bosnian hides it on the end of words like coffee.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because it keeps the word coffee the same in every job. You can say this is coffee and I want coffee without touching a single letter. You already do a tiny version of the Bosnian trick with people. You say I when you do the thing, and me when the thing happens to you. Coffee in English does not bother. Bosnian coffee does, so the list word kahva becomes kahvu when Ana wants the drink. That one change is not a tense, and it is not a new pile. It is a preview of work this book will unpack later.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already gave you a line you can say without a chart, and this book is the chart behind it. Ana wants coffee, so she says Želim kahvu instead of repeating the list word kahva. Today you only need the shock that the word changed. The rest of the book explains the change in pieces, one system at a time.
knownLine.speaker: Ana

pattern.heading: The map
pattern.body: This notebook teaches four big systems, then a last habit about little words, and it refuses to teach them on the same page. Piles file a word as he, she, or leftover. Jobs change the end of a thing-word when you name it, want it, have none of it, give it, or go with it. Matching words like my have to ride with that pile and that job. Doing-words change for time, and for whether the action is finished. Little words like se then sit in second place in the sentence. You will meet each system on its own day, with the same coffee, bridge, and house.

rows: He, she, leftover. File the word.
Name it, want it, none of it, to it, with it.
My has to ride with coffee.
Now, past, future, eat vs eat up.

howYouGuess.heading: How to use this book
howYouGuess.body: Use this book one system at a time, with a small chart, a few tries, and a check. The same coffee, bridge, house, Ana, and Emir come back in every chapter so you are not memorizing a new grocery list. You can start here without finishing Book 1, and the sentences will still make sense. If you already walked Book 1, you get a bonus because you have already said the line.

trick.heading: The mix-up to skip
trick.body: The trap is to call every change a tense. Tense is time on a doing-word, like now versus past. Most of the headache is not time. Thing-words change for the job in the sentence, and they also sit in a pile. Those are different systems. This book skips the tourist walk on purpose so the notebook can stay on those endings. There are no civic notes and no cat plot here, because Book 1 already owns that walk through town.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body:
Old English is not a class you missed. It is the English people actually spoke in England about a thousand years ago. Farmers, priests, and kings around Winchester used it. You do not speak it because languages keep changing. Parents slur, kids copy the slur, and after enough centuries the extra endings fall off. A later mix with French in England sped that wearing-down up, so the English in your mouth is the later, simpler version that won.

That older English hung extra letters on the end of a thing-word to show the job, the same habit Bosnian still has. You can still see a scrap of it when you say I if you do the thing and me if the thing happens to you. Coffee lost those outfits, so this is coffee and I want coffee stay the same. Bosnian never fired the endings on kahva. English moved the work off the word. Bosnian left it on.

items.speaker: Ana
items.english: That is coffee, still in the list form. Naming it is one job.

items.speaker: Ana
items.english: I want coffee, and the last letter moved. Wanting it is a later job, not a tense.

items.speaker: Emir
items.english: That is a bridge, still in the list form. Chapter 1 will file this word in a different pile from coffee.

items.speaker: Amira
items.english: That is a house, and this word will move later too. Same small set all book long.

items.prompt: In English, does coffee change when you want it?
items.explanation: I want coffee uses the same word as this is coffee.

items.prompt: In Želim kahvu, did kahva stay kahva?
items.explanation: It became kahvu because the job in the sentence changed. That job is not today’s chart.

items.prompt: Where does Bosnian put the work?
options: On the end of the word
items.explanation: The last letters move. English put the work in words like the and to.

items.prompt: Are the seven jobs on coffee the same thing as tenses?
options: Yes. Every change is a tense.
No. Tense is time on a doing-word.
items.explanation: Naming coffee versus wanting coffee is a job. Now versus past is tense.
Book 1 stays the story. Book 2 stays the later sequel. This is grammar.

items.prompt: What does this chapter teach you to do?
options: See the map, then wait for one system a day
items.explanation: The map is the point. Chapter 1 starts with piles.

items.prompt: Which system comes first after this map?
options: Piles. Why coffee is a she.
items.explanation: File the word before you change it.

items.prompt: The vocab list shows kahva. Is that the only form?
items.explanation: Želim kahvu is the same drink in a different outfit.

questions.question: Why does Bosnian feel harder than English at first?
options: The work sits on the end of the word
Every sentence needs a new vocab list
You must learn three languages at once
questions.explanation: English hid the work in little words. Bosnian left it on the thing-word.

questions.question: What is this chapter?
options: A full chart of every ending
questions.explanation: Piles, jobs, matching, and doing-words each get their own later chapter.

questions.question: In English, I want coffee uses the same coffee as this is coffee. What did Bosnian do?
options: It switched to a new drink
It moved the doing-word to the end
questions.explanation: Kahva became kahvu. Chapter 1 is the pile. Chapter 2 is that job.

questions.question: Why is naming coffee versus wanting coffee not a tense?
options: Because Bosnian has no time words
Tense is time on a doing-word. This is a job on coffee.
questions.explanation: Jobs live on thing-words. Tense lives on doing-words, later in the book.

questions.question: Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago. Why don’t you speak it?
options: It slowly wore down into the English you speak now.
questions.explanation: That older English put extra letters on thing-words. Yours mostly dropped them. Bosnian kept them.

questions.question: What comes next?
questions.explanation: You file the word first. Then the ending can be right.

next.body: You now have the map. Chapter 1 files coffee into a pile so later jobs can pick the right ending. That pile is why kahva is a she. You still will not get a seven-job chart tomorrow.
